title: The Cascade and Specificity
summary: When two rules target the same element, the cascade decides which wins — through origin, importance, specificity, and source order, in that exact priority. Learn the tuple model and taming it with layers instead of !important.

slides.markdown:
"Why isn't my style applying?" is one of the most common CSS debugging sessions there is, and almost every time, the answer is: **a more powerful rule is winning, and you haven't found it yet.**

CSS never asks "which rule was written more recently" as its first question. It runs competing declarations through an ordered set of tiebreakers — origin, importance, specificity, source order — and only moves to the next tiebreaker when the current one is a tie. Knowing that order cold turns a guessing exercise into a five-second lookup.

This topic covers that order precisely, how to calculate specificity without guessing, and the layers system that lets large codebases avoid the specificity wars entirely.

slides.subTitle: Origin, importance, specificity, source order
slides.markdown:
When two declarations target the same property on the same element, the browser resolves the conflict through four tiebreakers, checked **in this exact order** — it only looks at the next one if the current one is tied:

1. **Origin and importance** — user-agent styles lose to author (your) styles, which lose to `!important` author styles, which lose to `!important` user styles. (Full order: user-agent → author → author `!important` → user `!important`.)
2. **Specificity** — a numeric weight calculated from the selector itself (next slide).
3. **Source order** — if origin and specificity are both tied, whichever rule appears **later** in the stylesheet (or later `<style>`/`<link>`) wins.

Most day-to-day "why didn't my style apply" bugs are actually specificity ties broken by source order, or specificity mismatches that look like ties at a glance but aren't. Knowing which tiebreaker you're looking at is the whole debugging skill.

slides.subTitle: The (a, b, c) tuple
slides.markdown:
Specificity is a three-part tuple, compared left to right — a higher value in an earlier position always wins, regardless of how large the later positions are:

- **a** — number of ID selectors (`#header`)
- **b** — number of class selectors, attribute selectors, and pseudo-classes (`.card`, `[type="text"]`, `:hover`)
- **c** — number of element (type) selectors and pseudo-elements (`div`, `::before`)

`#nav .item` is `(1, 1, 0)`. `.nav .item .link .icon` is `(0, 3, 0)` — three classes, no ID — and loses to the first selector even though it has more total selectors, because the tuple compares position by position, not by adding everything into one number. A single ID always beats any number of classes; a single class always beats any number of element selectors.

Inline `style=""` attributes outrank every selector-based rule (effectively above the tuple entirely), and `!important` outranks even that — both bypass the tuple system rather than scoring high within it.

Take two competing rules targeting the same button: `.sidebar .btn.primary` and `#app button.cta`. At a glance the second looks stronger because it has an ID — but walk the tuple to be sure rather than eyeballing it.

`.sidebar .btn.primary` — zero IDs, three classes (`.sidebar`, `.btn`, `.primary`), zero elements → `(0, 3, 0)`.
`#app button.cta` — one ID (`#app`), one class (`.cta`), one element (`button`) → `(1, 1, 1)`.

Comparing left to right: `a` is 1 vs 0 — the second rule wins outright at the very first position, and the fact that the first rule has three classes to the second's one is irrelevant, because the comparison never reaches position `b`.

slides.sectionTitle: !important as an escape hatch, not a tool
slides.markdown:
`!important` bypasses the specificity comparison entirely — an `!important` declaration beats every normal-importance declaration regardless of selector weight, and among multiple `!important` declarations, the normal specificity/source-order rules apply again, just at that elevated importance tier.

The pitfall is what it does to a codebase over time: once one `!important` is added to force a style through, the *next* person who needs to override that gets one option that reliably works — another `!important`, at higher specificity or later in source order. This escalates. Real legacy codebases end up with `!important` stacked on `!important`, at which point specificity as a concept stops being reasoned about at all, and every override is trial and error.

The honest fix when you reach for `!important` is almost always to ask why the original rule's specificity was set too high or too broad in the first place, and fix that instead — `!important` should be reserved for utility classes deliberately designed to always win (like a `.hidden` visibility utility) or third-party CSS you can't edit directly.

slides.subTitle: Taming specificity wars in large codebases
Which properties inherit by default
slides.markdown:
Inheritance is a separate mechanism from the cascade — it's what happens *after* the cascade resolves a value for an element's parent, deciding whether a child that has no competing rule of its own picks up that resolved value.

Typography-related properties inherit by default — `color`, `font-family`, `font-size`, `line-height`, `text-align` — because it would be absurd to have to re-declare font family on every nested `<span>`. Box-model and layout properties do **not** inherit by default — `margin`, `padding`, `border`, `width`, `display` — because a child having the same margin as its parent would rarely make layout sense.

Three keywords give explicit control regardless of the default: `inherit` (force inheritance even on a normally non-inheriting property), `initial` (reset to the property's spec-defined default, ignoring both cascade and inheritance), and `unset` (acts like `inherit` on naturally-inheriting properties, `initial` on the rest) — useful when resetting a component's styles without knowing which properties would otherwise inherit stray values from an ancestor.

The fastest way to answer "why isn't my style applying" is the browser devtools **Computed** panel, not re-reading the stylesheet from the top.

```
1. Inspect the element.
2. Open the "Computed" tab (not just "Styles").
3. Find the property in question and click the arrow next to its value —
   devtools lists every rule that set that property, in cascade-resolution
   order, with the winning one at top and losers struck through.
```

This single workflow directly answers the question devtools' regular "Styles" panel only hints at: it shows you *which selector actually won* and, critically, whether the loser lost on specificity or got beaten later in source order — both show up as strikethrough, but hovering each struck-through rule's selector reveals its specificity tuple, letting you compare directly instead of guessing.

Most "CSS is broken" reports resolve in under a minute once you check Computed instead of scanning source files by eye.

A specificity mismatch between a design system's base components and an app's override styles is one of the most common real-world sources of "I set the style but nothing changed" bugs — the library author didn't do anything wrong, but their internal selectors (often nested, sometimes ID-based for legacy reasons) can out-specificity a simple override class.

This is exactly why utility-first CSS (Tailwind-style) and CSS Modules both deliberately keep every generated selector at the same, low specificity — usually a single class, `(0, 1, 0)` — so that no override fight is even possible; the last one applied in source order always wins cleanly. It's also why `@layer` has become popular for shipping component libraries: the library wraps its own styles in a named layer, and consumers' plain unlayered CSS automatically outranks anything inside a named layer, regardless of selector weight, by cascade-layer rules alone.

Understanding this is what lets you diagnose a "the library's CSS won't let me override it" ticket as a specificity or layering problem in seconds, rather than reaching for `!important` as a first move.

A complete answer to "why isn't my CSS applying" walks the cascade in order rather than guessing at any one step:

1. **Check origin/importance first** — is a user-agent default or an `!important` somewhere in play?
2. **Compute both selectors' specificity tuples** — don't eyeball it, count IDs, classes, and elements explicitly.
3. **If specificity is tied, check source order** — later wins.
4. **If layers are involved, check those before specificity at all** — a later layer beats an earlier one unconditionally.

Saying this sequence out loud, in order, while pointing at the devtools Computed panel to confirm each step, reads as someone who has actually debugged this dozens of times — versus someone reaching for `!important` on instinct because a style "isn't working."
